subject: mathematics
question_text: Prove that the smaller angle θ between any two diagonals of a cube is given by cos θ = 1/3.

mark_split.label: Set up a unit cube on the axes
Write the two diagonals as vectors
Apply the cosine formula and simplify

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.64 — SAQ chapter 9 Product of Vectors, answer 62. Printed appearances: AP 17. The only PROOF in this chapter and the only answer with a figure. The book notes the same question appears in Maths-1B. It is proved on a UNIT cube because the angle does not depend on the size — a choice worth stating rather than assuming.⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed against this answer. It is not a bare guess: this same chapter DOES print splits for answers 58 and 59 on book p.63 (1+1+1+1) and for answer 61 on p.64 (1+2+1), so the shape used here is the chapter's own. The book's chapter header carries ★★ and reads '4 Marks'; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B runs Q11-Q17 at 4 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q13 is the Product of Vectors slot.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — say what cube you set up and which two diagonals you take.

steps.label: Set up a unit cube
steps.margin_note: First mark. Put one corner at the origin and three edges along the axes. A UNIT cube is enough: scaling a cube does not change the angle between its diagonals.
steps.memory_tip: A UNIT cube is enough — scaling a cube does not change the angle between its diagonals.
lines: Consider a unit cube with vertices O, A, B, C,
M, N, P, L placed on the coordinate axes,
We take OA = i, OB = j, OC = k.

recall.must_convey: That a unit cube is set up with one corner at the origin and edges i, j, k along the axes.
accept: take a unit cube with a corner at the origin and edges along i j and k
set up the cube on the coordinate axes with unit edges
let OA be i, OB be j and OC be k
unit cube ni origin daggara petti, edges i j k ga teeskuntam
place the cube on the axes with one vertex at O

steps.why: The angle between diagonals is the same for every cube, so choosing side 1 loses no generality and makes every vector a sum of unit vectors.
common_mistakes: Using a cube of side a and carrying it through pointlessly.
Placing the cube off the axes, which makes the vectors messy.

steps.label: Draw the cube
steps.margin_note: Worth no mark but worth drawing. Mark the two diagonals OP and CL — with them on the page you can read their components straight off instead of deriving them.
steps.memory_tip: With OP and CL drawn, their components can be read off instead of derived.

recall.must_convey: That a labelled cube is drawn with the two diagonals marked. Naming the drawing is full credit — it cannot be spoken.
accept: draw the cube and mark the two diagonals OP and CL
sketch the labelled cube with its diagonals
make a diagram showing the cube and the two space diagonals
cube geesi rendu diagonals OP and CL mark cheyyali
draw a labelled cube with the diagonals shown

steps.why: A space diagonal runs from a corner to the corner diagonally opposite through the middle. The picture is how you check you have picked two such diagonals and not a face diagonal.
common_mistakes: Taking a face diagonal, which gives a different angle.
Labelling the vertices so that OP and CL are the same diagonal.

steps.label: Write the diagonals
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Walk each diagonal edge by edge and add the steps. OP goes along i, then j, then k; CL goes along i, then j, then BACK along k — hence the minus.
steps.memory_tip: Walk each diagonal edge by edge. OP goes i, j, k; CL goes i, j, then BACK along k — hence the minus.
lines: Consider the diagonals OP and CL.
OP = OA + AL + LP = i + j + k   …(1)
CL = CN + NP + PL = i + j − k   …(2)

recall.must_convey: That OP = i + j + k and CL = i + j − k, the minus arising because that diagonal runs back along the k direction.
accept: OP is i plus j plus k and CL is i plus j minus k
walk each diagonal along the edges and add, one has a minus k
the two diagonals are i plus j plus k and i plus j minus k
OP i plus j plus k, CL i plus j minus k, minus vasthundi
add the edge steps to get each diagonal

steps.why: Every space diagonal of a unit cube has components ±1, ±1, ±1. Two different diagonals differ in exactly one sign, and that single sign is what produces the 1/3.
common_mistakes: Giving both diagonals as i + j + k, which are the same line.
Losing the minus on the k component.

steps.label: Apply the cosine formula
steps.margin_note: Half the marks. The dot product gives 1 + 1 − 1 = 1, and each magnitude is √3, so the denominator is 3. Both diagonals have the same length, which is what makes it so clean.
steps.memory_tip: The dot gives 1 + 1 − 1 = 1 and each magnitude is √3, so the denominator is 3.

recall.must_convey: That cos θ is the dot product over the product of the magnitudes, giving (1+1−1)/(√3·√3) = 1/3.
accept: cos theta is the dot product over the two magnitudes, one plus one minus one over three which is one third
the dot product is one and each magnitude is root three so cos theta is one third
apply the cosine formula to get one over three
dot product one, magnitudes root three each, cos theta one by three
the answer is cos theta equals one third

steps.why: The two diagonals agree in two components and differ in one, so the dot product is 1 + 1 − 1 = 1 while each length stays √3. That is the whole reason the answer is exactly a third.
common_mistakes: Adding the magnitudes instead of multiplying them.
Getting the dot product as 3 by ignoring the minus sign.
Reporting the angle instead of its cosine when the cosine was asked for.

insider_note: Choose a UNIT cube with one corner at the origin so every component is 1 or −1. The two diagonals differ in a single sign, which is what leaves 1 + 1 − 1 = 1 over 3.
